line:
I take breakfast with Lady Maren and ask for one thing: let me tell her village the truth about the ford hero myself, in the Heron and Net's common room, at midday. A confession from the storyteller who found the page would sting less than one from an assessor, and it would give me a crowd of honest witnesses at my back before dusk.

In the afternoon I'll scout the ford and its stepping stones, pick a spot where I can speak with Corvin in the open with Hob Crannock and a few villagers within earshot, and ask Lady Maren to lend me two of her men-at-arms to stand quietly in the willows.

input.add_to_description: Day 5 midday: Wren's confession in the Heron and Net went badly (nat 1): she tangled her words, the crowd heard "the Thistlewoods lied" more than "a stranger exposed it", and a loud blacksmith, Dunstan Rook, now wants the toll struck and Lady Maren's hide. Lady Maren's two men-at-arms (Pell and Harrow) were lent to Wren anyway. Afternoon scouting: Wren spotted the willows on the far bank have been trampled, and a fresh wagon-rut leads to a hollow behind them: Corvin's men are already in position.

entries.text: notebook: updated Ashby Weir
time: 9 hours 30 minutes later: Day 5, 4:30 PM

Breakfast with Lady Maren is quiet. She hears your request, goes pale, and agrees. "Better from you than from a stranger with a seal," she says, and lends you two of her men-at-arms, Pell and Harrow.

Midday at the Heron and Net goes badly. You stand on a bench with the common room packed, and your Performance check is a natural 1. Your tongue trips, a pun lands wrong, and what the crowd hears is "the Thistlewoods lied for twenty years" and not "a swindler fooled them." A blacksmith named Dunstan Rook bellows that the toll must go and the Lady with it. Hob Crannock tries to speak and is shouted down. Pell and Harrow hustle you out, and the village is angrier at the spur than it was this morning. That is a mess you will need to mend.

The afternoon is kinder. Your Perception check at the ford is a 14. The stepping stones cross a shallow bar about forty paces wide, with a gravel spit mid-stream where you could talk in the open. But on the far bank the willows are trampled, and a fresh wagon-rut leads into a hollow behind them. Corvin's people are already in place, hours before dusk.

It's half past four. Dusk is about two hours away. Pell and Harrow wait by the cottage with Hob. Dunstan Rook's angry crowd mutters at the inn.

What does Wren do?

sheet.name: Wren Ashgrove
sheet.opening: Wren Ashgrove, a half-elf bard of about nineteen with a quick grin and a sharper tongue, arrives at dusk in the river-market town of Marrowford, a few weeks after fleeing the caravan of her mentor Corvin Tallowmere. She was raised by him as a storyteller's apprentice, and she left in the night at a river crossing with his ledger of forged tales sold to nobles (its pages now hidden in the binding of her road-psalter), a few of his best forgeries, and a head start. She carries a brass lantern-shaped reliquary of the Lantern-Bearer, a gentle road-god of travelers and tale-tellers whom Corvin worshipped only as cover; it holds a curl of yellowed parchment in an unknown hand that may be a true blessing or another forgery. She does not know if Corvin has sent anyone after her. Her ideal: stories should be free, and truth is whatever people can be made to believe. Her bond: find the nobles Corvin cheated and decide whether to expose him or quietly fix what he did. Her flaw: she can't resist a secret, and she lies even when the truth would serve her better. She has 15 gp, a rapier, a dagger, leather armor, a lute, a diplomat's pack with blank paper and sealing wax, and was raised with no memory of her birth family. The hook: as she reaches the market square, she spots a caravan wagon with Corvin's painted shrine-lantern sigil parked at the edge of town, but no sign of Corvin. A frightened young page in a minor noble's livery is pressing a sealed letter into the hands of the wagon's driver, and the seal looks like one Wren has seen in the ledger. Something is happening that links her stolen ledger to a noble house, and it needs a quick-witted liar to either sort it out or be caught in it. Open on Wren in the square, with the choice of how to approach the wagon and the page, and a locked iron-bound strongbox on the wagon's tailboard that she itches to poke at.

input.add_to_description: Day 5 midday: Wren told the village in the Heron and Net that the ford hero was Corvin's invention; with Lady Maren beside her, the villagers accepted a plan to renegotiate the toll fairly. Afternoon scouting (Perception 19): Garrow lies hidden in the willows on the far bank, and the wagon is parked in a dry hollow behind the old weir-keeper's hut with the driver dozing. Chosen meeting spot: the middle stepping stones, within earshot of Hob's cottage green and the near bank.

entries.text: notebook: updated Ashby Weir
time: 9 hours 30 minutes later: Day 5, 4:30 PM

Lady Maren hears your request over porridge and doesn't argue. "Say it in my name as well," she says. "I'd rather be ashamed with company."

At noon the Heron and Net is packed to the rafters, with fishermen, weavers, the ferryman, and a dozen children on the stairs. Your Performance check was a 22. You tell it as a story, because that's what you are: the hero at the ford, the grand painting, the tale a clever man sold to a frightened family. You make them laugh at the tidy hero, then you let the laughter go quiet, and you say the true part plainly. The toll was never his to give, and the lady never knew. Lady Maren stands beside you and says, "I did not ask, and I should have." Nobody shouts. The ferryman scratches his chin and says the toll can be talked about like honest folk, and a murmur of agreement goes round. It isn't forgiveness yet, but it is a start.

In the afternoon you walk the ford. Your Perception check was a 19. Across the water in the willows, a brown coat lies still in the reeds, Garrow, watching. Behind the old weir-keeper's hut, in a dry hollow, the painted wagon stands with its driver dozing on the box. No Corvin yet. You pick the middle stepping stones as your ground, open to the water, in earshot of Hob's green door and the near bank. Hob promises to sit on his step with his pipe, and Lady Maren lends you two men-at-arms, who settle quietly into the willows on the near side.

It is half past four on Day 5. Dusk is a couple of hours off. Garrow doesn't know you've seen him.

What does Wren do?

input.add_to_description: Day 5 noon: Wren (Performance 24) confessed the forged ford-hero tale in the Heron and Net. The village listened, then laughed with relief and cheered; the miller's wife proposed settling the toll by a shared village-and-manor ferry committee. Lady Maren agreed publicly. Day 5 afternoon: Wren's Perception (4) at the ford missed that Garrow lies hidden in the reed-bed upstream of the stepping stones with a crossbow-less cudgel, waiting for dusk; two of Lady Maren's men-at-arms (Dunstan and Pell's nephew Joss) are posted in the willows.

entries.text: notebook: updated Ashby Weir
sheet: XP +50: 225
time: 9 hours 30 minutes later: Day 5, 4:30 PM

Lady Maren hears your request over porridge, sets down her spoon, and says, "My mother would have liked that. Do it." She sends a boy running ahead to the Heron and Net.

At noon the common room is packed to the rafters: fishermen, the miller and his wife, a blacksmith with arms like hams, children on the stairs. You stand on a bench with your lute and tell it straight. Your Performance check was a 24. You tell them the ford hero never held any ford, that a clever man sold the tale to a frightened family, and that the toll you've quarrelled over for twenty years rested on a lie that nobody here made. The room is silent. Then the miller's wife laughs, a big, relieved bark, and the whole room breaks. Lady Maren, standing at the back, agrees aloud to a shared ferry-committee of village and manor. People shake your hand. You've earned 50 XP, bringing you to 225 of 300.

In the afternoon you walk the ford. The stepping stones are broad and flat, the water shin-deep and fast, the willows thick on the near bank. You choose a flat shelf of rock mid-ford where Hob's cottage and the village green are both within earshot. Lady Maren lends you two men-at-arms, Dunstan and young Joss, who settle quietly into the willows with bows unstrung. Your Perception check was a 4, so you're sure of the ground and nothing else. The reed-bed upstream looks like reeds, and that's all you can say about it.

It's half past four on Day 5. Dusk is a couple of hours off. Hob has taken a stool outside his green door with his pipe. The light is turning gold, and the wagon has not yet appeared.

What does Wren do until dusk?

input.add_to_description: Day 5 midday: Wren confessed the forged ford tale in the Heron and Net (Performance 19). The villagers, led by the miller Dunstan Hale-Wick's widow Bess, accepted Lady Maren's offer to settle the toll by village moot rather than by the forged claim. Wren chose a meeting spot on the ford's western gravel bar, visible from Hob's cottage and the inn; two men-at-arms (Pell and Harrick) wait in the willows. Wren's Perception (5) missed Garrow, who lies hidden in the reeds upstream of the weir.

entries.text: notebook: updated Ashby Weir
sheet: XP +50: 225
time: 9 hours 30 minutes later: Day 5, 4:30 PM

Lady Maren listens over porridge, then slowly smiles. "My mother would have called that either very brave or very vain. I'll take brave." She agrees on the spot.

At noon the Heron and Net is packed, with fishers, weavers, and boys perched on the rafters. You stand on a bench with your lute and tell them the story of the hero at the ford, all of it, the handsome lie and the page that records its sale. Your Performance check was a 19. You make them laugh at the tidy man in the painting, and then you make the laughter stop. When you finish, nobody shouts. A broad miller's widow named Bess rises and says that if the lady will settle the toll at a village moot, fairly, she'll sit at it. Lady Maren, standing at the back, bows her head and says yes. That's worth 50 XP, bringing you to 225 of 300.

In the afternoon you walk the ford with Hob leaning on your arm. You choose the western gravel bar, open and in plain sight of his cottage door and the inn's yard, with the stepping stones leading to it. Two of Lady Maren's men-at-arms, Pell and Harrick, drift into the willows with ale-jugs to look idle. Your Perception check was only a 5, so you check the reeds and the weir and see nothing but heron-prints. That doesn't mean there's nothing there.

It's half past four. Dusk is about two hours off. The village has quietly gathered on the inn's green, pretending not to watch the water.

What does Wren do?

features: Darkvision: You have superior vision in dark and dim conditions. You can see in dim light within 60 feet of you as if it were bright light, and in darkness as if it were dim light. You cannot discern color in darkness, only shades of gray.
Fey Ancestry: You have advantage on saving throws against being charmed, and magic cannot put you to sleep.
Skill Versatility: You gain proficiency in two skills of your choice.

Bardic Inspiration (d6): You can inspire others through stirring words or music. To do so, you use a bonus action on your turn to choose one creature other than yourself within 60 feet of you who can hear you. That creature gains one Bardic Inspiration die, a d6. Once within the next 10 minutes, the creature can roll the die and add the number rolled to one ability check, attack roll, or saving throw it makes. The creature can wait until after it rolls the d20 before deciding to use the Bardic Inspiration die, but must decide before the GM says whether the roll succeeds or fails. Once the Bardic Inspiration die is rolled, it is lost. A creature can have only one Bardic Inspiration die at a time. You can use this feature a number of times equal to your Charisma modifier (a minimum of once). You regain any expended uses when you finish a long rest.  Your Bardic Inspiration die changes when you reach certain levels in this class. The die becomes a d8 at 5th level, a d10 at 10th level, and a d12 at 15th level.

Shelter of the Faithful (Acolyte): As an acolyte, you command the respect of those who share your faith, and you can perform the religious ceremonies of your deity. You and your adventuring companions can expect to receive free healing and care at a temple, shrine, or other established presence of your faith, though you must provide any material components needed for spells. Those who share your religion will support you (but only you) at a modest lifestyle. You might also have ties to a specific temple dedicated to your chosen deity or pantheon, and you have a residence there. This could be the temple where you used to serve, if you remain on good terms with it, or a temple where you have found a new home. While near your temple, you can call upon the priests for assistance, provided the assistance you ask for is not hazardous and you remain in good standing with your temple.

spellcasting.notes: Spells known are fixed until a level-up.
